PullRequest.Title: sessions: nest automatic sections inside custom groups
PullRequest.Body:

## Summary

Allows an entire workspace, repository, or environment section to live inside a custom group in the Agents window's sessions list.

- Drag section headings into custom groups or subgroups, reorder them alongside child groups, and return them to the top level.
- Provides keyboard-accessible Move to Group / Remove from Group context-menu actions with focus restoration.
- Persists section placement separately for each grouping mode, including Repository mode's workspace fallback. Future matching sessions follow their section; pins and explicit session memberships retain precedence.
- Keeps placement and mixed child ordering in the groups service, top-level ordering in the section-order service, and mode-dependent presentation in the list.
- Builds group presentation once after section placement so totals, nesting depths, comparison-group placement, and bulk actions agree.
- Offers Undo when group deletion releases nested sections and restores section placement unless it has since moved to another group.
- Adds service/UI regressions and updates accessibility help and the sessions-list contract.

## Stack

Second of two feature PRs, stacked on #343240. This targets `benibenj/agents/group-sessions-by-environment`, not `main`, so its diff contains only section nesting and the related architecture/reliability improvements. Merge #343240 first, then retarget this PR to `main`.

## How to test

1. In the Agents window, create a custom group and optionally a subgroup.
2. Group sessions by Workspace, Repository, or Environment and drag an automatic section into that custom group. Verify indentation, counts, ordering, and collapsed destinations.
3. Use the section's Move to Group / Remove from Group context-menu actions, including a destination with collapsed ancestors and an older section hidden by Recent capping when top-level.
4. Switch grouping modes and back. Verify each mode remembers its own placement, new matching sessions follow the section, and pins/explicit memberships keep precedence.
5. Exercise group bulk actions and comparison groups inside nested sections. Delete the parent and use Undo to restore its sections and mixed child order.

## Validation

- `git diff --check 16266fd5eab..e85a5e114f6` — passed.
- Actual group-service runtime checks — passed mixed ordering, persistence without session membership, empty catalogs, delete/undo, newer-placement preservation, and return to top level; 350 deterministic mixed moves and 14 persistence round trips also passed.
- Isolated stacked snapshot — TypeScript syntax checks and internal dependency bundling passed for six relevant test entry points. External packages were excluded; these are not executed unit tests or a TypeScript type check.
- `npm run build-fast -- --client-only` — blocked: missing root `node_modules/gulp/bin/gulp.js`. Earlier dependency restoration with `npm run install-fast` failed with registry authentication `E401`.
- Full unit tests, ESLint, TypeScript type checking, and live UI validation were not completed because the required dependencies are unavailable.
- Focused suites to run once dependencies are restored: `./scripts/test.sh --run src/vs/sessions/services/sessions/test/browser/sessionGroupsService.test.ts --run src/vs/sessions/contrib/sessions/test/browser/sessionsList.test.ts --run src/vs/sessions/contrib/sessions/test/browser/sessionsListContextMenu.test.ts --run src/vs/sessions/contrib/sessions/test/browser/sessionsArchiveActions.test.ts` — not run.

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: The recursive call count, full-map scans, prior indexed lookup, and synchronous update call paths are explicit in code. Only the exact user group count and resulting milliseconds are workload-dependent.
Findings.PerformanceResource: Synchronous CPU work and temporary arrays while rebuilding the sessions tree
Findings.PerformanceScaling: For G rendered custom groups and K nested-section memberships, this invokes getChildIds G times; each invocation filters all G groups, scans all K section memberships, and sorts the matching children, making the new work O(G² + G*K) per list update.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: Increased synchronous list-update latency and UI jank
Findings.PreviousBehavior: A single SessionGroupTree was built for the update, and each group's children were read from its parent index in O(1), yielding an O(G) traversal (apart from unrelated session work).
Findings.ChangedBehavior: Rendering now calls ISessionGroupsService.getChildIds for every group. That helper rebuilds each result by filtering [..._groups.values()], calling getSectionIdsInGroup (which scans _sectionMembership), and sorting.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: The added call at line 5346 is inside recursive renderGroup, so it runs once for every rendered custom group. The deleted code used groupTree.getSubgroups(groupId), whose SessionGroupTree pre-indexes children by parent.
Findings.Title: Avoid rescanning every group for each rendered group
Findings.Impact: With many custom groups, any visible Agents Sessions list refresh performs quadratic group scans on the UI path, causing increasingly slow updates and interaction jank even when no sections are nested.
Findings.Evidence: SessionsList.update synchronously builds children before tree.setChildren and is reached by session changes, active-session changes, filters, group changes, and order changes. renderGroup recursively visits every custom group. SessionGroupsService.getChildIds at lines 520-525 filters the complete group map and calls the linear getSectionIdsInGroup at lines 516-518 on each visit, while SessionGroupTree.getSubgroups is backed by subgroupsByParentId.
Findings.Recommendation: Build the mixed child-id lists once per SessionsList.update from the existing groupTree plus one section-by-parent index, or maintain equivalent indexes in SessionGroupsService, then have renderGroup consume those precomputed lists.

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: The expanded selection, Promise.all fan-out, and provider/IPC path are directly traced. The number of unread sessions and backend sensitivity vary, which limits severity rather than confidence in the mechanism.
Findings.PerformanceResource: Concurrent per-session provider calls and agent-host IPC dispatches
Findings.PerformanceScaling: One group action now selects every unread, unpinned session in every automatic section nested anywhere in the group subtree. For N such sessions, markAllRead starts N setSessionReadState calls concurrently, and agent-host sessions can additionally dispatch per unread chat.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: A catalog-sized IPC burst, provider contention, refresh-event pressure, and degraded action/UI latency
Findings.PreviousBehavior: The group action passed only sessions with explicit membership in the custom-group subtree. Automatic sections had separate per-section actions, so one group action did not aggregate several sections' catalogs.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: A single Mark All as Read on a parent group can now aggregate all unread sessions from all nested automatic sections and pass that expanded set to the existing unbounded bulk implementation.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: The added condition at line 7182 expands the existing group bulk action beyond explicit group memberships to all sessions whose section parent is in groupIds; one group may contain multiple workspace, repository, or environment sections.
Findings.Title: Bound bulk read-state updates for nested sections
Findings.Impact: When a user nests several active repository/workspace/environment sections under one group and chooses Mark All as Read, the action can immediately fan out across the full unread catalog, overwhelming remote/provider channels and triggering a burst of list updates.
Findings.Evidence: getMarkAllSessionsReadAction passes the selected array to ISessionsManagementService.markAllRead. SessionsManagementService.markAllRead at line 1432 uses Promise.all(sessions.map(setSessionReadState)); setSessionReadState calls the provider once per session, and BaseAgentHostSessionsProvider.setSessionReadState emits change events and connection.dispatch IPC for changed sessions, with additional per-chat calls for aggregate unread chats. No limiter or provider grouping bounds aggregate concurrency.
Findings.Recommendation: Run the expanded set through a bounded-concurrency executor (preferably in the shared markAllRead implementation) while preserving the returned promise's completion semantics; use a provider batch API only if one actually exists.

Scenarios.Scenario: Visible Agents Sessions list rebuild after session, active-session, filter, grouping, or order changes
Scenarios.CriticalPath: SessionsList.update synchronously filters and sections the catalog, builds group presentation, recursively renders every group, then calls tree.setChildren; all changed group-child discovery is on the UI critical path.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: G custom groups, K persisted automatic-section placements, S sessions, and the visible tree rows. The reported added child lookup costs O(G² + G*K) after effective grouping.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Single-threaded synchronous tree-model construction. Chat-observable updates are animation-frame scheduled, but many management, model, group, order, and filter events call update directly; there is no parallelism or backpressure within one rebuild.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: A fresh SessionGroupTree indexes group children once per update, but the changed render path bypasses that index and reconstructs each group's mixed children by rescanning service maps. Warm storage/cache state does not avoid those scans.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: recursive call count, service scan implementation, prior indexed behavior, and synchronous reachability are explicit.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: The exact number of custom groups and frame time varies by user; the quadratic mechanism applies even with no nested sections and becomes visible as group count grows.
Scenarios.Verdict: Reportable repeated-work regression: the diff replaces indexed child lookup with one full group/section scan per rendered group.

Scenarios.Scenario: Drag or context-menu move of an automatic workspace/repository/environment section
Scenarios.CriticalPath: moveHeader calls SessionGroupsService.moveSection, which updates placement, serializes group state, stores it, fires onDidChange, and synchronously rebuilds the visible list; returning a section to top level also reorders top-level section state.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Persist the complete profile-scoped session-groups JSON state through IStorageService.store
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One store per section move; returning to top level may also cause one separate section-order persistence operation.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Automatic sections could only be reordered at top level through the section-order service; no group-membership snapshot was stored for section nesting. Group moves already persisted one groups snapshot.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The group-state store occurs before the service change event and visible list update complete.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: One moved section; serialized state grows with groups, explicit session memberships, section memberships, and stored child-order entries.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: One synchronous user action. Storage writes and the resulting update are serialized; no fan-out occurs.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Placement is held in in-memory maps after load. Every actual move persists a full JSON snapshot; no write coalescing is used, but the action cardinality is one and moves are user-paced.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High for the one full-state serialization/store; low concern because cardinality is bounded to the user action.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Storage backend duration and state size vary, but moves are explicit and infrequent.
Scenarios.Verdict: No additional finding: persistence is required, user-paced, and does not fan out.

Scenarios.Scenario: Mark All as Read on a custom group containing automatic sections
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The group action scans current sessions, includes sessions from nested automatic sections, then awaits SessionsManagementService.markAllRead; that method immediately starts one provider setSessionReadState promise per selected session.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Per-session provider setSessionReadState, including agent-host connection.dispatch updates and possible per-chat dispatches
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Exactly one provider call for each of N selected unread sessions, plus up to each agent-host session's unread aggregate-chat count; all N session calls start concurrently.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: A custom-group action selected only explicit group memberships. Automatic-section actions handled one section at a time; the group action could not aggregate multiple automatic sections.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The action promise waits for all provider calls, and provider change events can drive visible-list refresh work while the burst is in progress.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: N unread, unarchived, unpinned sessions across every automatic section nested anywhere in the selected group subtree, after section/group placement precedence. Agent-host sessions may contain multiple unread aggregate chats per session.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Promise.all creates effective concurrency N across sessions with no shared limiter; individual agent-host sessions may sequentially dispatch additional chat updates, while different sessions remain concurrent.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Sessions and provider objects are warm in memory, but read-state calls are neither deduplicated across the selected set nor coalesced/batched by provider. Empty/already-read sessions are filtered before the boundary.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: the changed inclusion condition, Promise.all implementation, and concrete agent-host IPC path are directly traced.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Unread catalog size, provider implementation, and remote latency vary; those affect severity, not the unbounded fan-out mechanism.
Scenarios.Verdict: Reportable concurrency-burst regression because one newly broadened group action can issue catalog-sized concurrent provider/IPC work.

Scenarios.Scenario: Delete a custom group containing subgroups and nested automatic sections, then Undo
Scenarios.CriticalPath: deleteGroup captures child orders and section placements, removes affected mappings, serializes once, updates the list, and optionally restoreGroups rebuilds mappings, serializes once, and restores top-level position.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Persist updated group/section placement state on delete and again on Undo restore
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One storage snapshot for delete and one for an invoked Undo, independent of subtree item count.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Group delete and restore already persisted one complete snapshot each; the diff adds section-placement entries to the same operations without adding per-section stores.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Persistence precedes each corresponding change event/list rebuild.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Deleted subtree group count, explicit session memberships, nested-section placements, and child-order entries.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Synchronous linear scans followed by one storage operation per delete or restore; user-paced and serialized.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: All group and membership state is in memory; deletion/restore scans maps and writes a complete snapshot. No repeated retries or retained undo cache beyond the notification-owned deleted snapshot.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High for bounded linear work and constant boundary-call count.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Large manually-created group trees increase linear scan and snapshot size, but actions are infrequent.
Scenarios.Verdict: No finding: section handling preserves one-store-per-action behavior and adds only linear in-memory work.

Analysis.Summary: Completed the performance pass over all 10 changed files. Reported one synchronous quadratic group-rendering regression and one unbounded provider/IPC burst from broadened group bulk actions; section persistence and delete/undo remain bounded, user-paced operations.
